The finance director stopped the slides on page four.

She asked what happens when the person who championed us leaves. I had no answer.

That question changed how I scope every renewal now.

A cold email landed in my inbox addressed to Ben.

My name isn't Ben. Eye roll.

I read the whole thing anyway.

Underneath the wrong name sat a business case for why a security vendor would be a good fit for one account, built out of that account's own internal initiatives.

Then this: "this is one of thousands. want the rest?"

And the sign off: "If this isn't useful, just say so and I'll stop."

Useful prospect research, handed over with nothing attached to it.

It's the thing I argue for, so being on the receiving end of it was a strange way to be convinced.

Lead with inherent value, ask for nothing back, and the dynamic flips.

The part I keep turning over is what someone would have to know about an account before they could write that email at all.

Clinicians aren't heavily on LinkedIn. The tools are built on LinkedIn, so for this market the filters had nothing underneath them.

So we went and got it by hand. Booking websites first, then the individual practice websites where the clinicians are listed.

This might be the boring version of the lesson, but the data was sitting on public pages the whole time.

Custom data gathering is more accessible than it has ever been.

Tools like ZoomInfo probably cost tens of thousands of dollars a year.

Most of my TAM builds now cost under $15 each.

They average 5,481 businesses per vertical. One client's verdict: "this is the most complete picture we've ever had of these verticals."

I've only been building them this way for six months. The better part of 10 years of TAMs before that all fell woefully short.

I'd call tools like ZoomInfo the legacy way to build a TAM. The tools don't have the coverage, and they define things in their own ways, so a TAM built from them can only be split by the filters they offer. I've got my own definitions, and I want the build to use them.

Once I went to other sources, I was seeing decision makers and businesses I couldn't see on those tools.

This probably works best for anyone selling into SMB.

Here's my system:

- Decide the boundaries first, including my own definition of the thing we're looking for.
- Work out how I want to split the vertical up.
- Go and find the businesses that fit that definition. Mostly that's their own websites, with LinkedIn and booking platforms on top.
- Then work out the shape of the TAM. Headcount from the people named on each website, who the decision maker is, whether they run software we can detect, and a few other things.

What makes this possible now is the tooling. I use Claude Code to pull it all together, but any tool that can do the same job would work.

Here's my system:

First, define what you're looking for.
- The boundaries: what's in and what's out.
- Your own definition, so you're not relying on someone else's.
- How you want to split the vertical up.

Then go and find the businesses that fit.
- Start with whoever licenses, funds or regulates them. They often have to publish a list, and that list becomes your backbone.
- Fill the gaps. Government directories and industry bodies. Maps listings and booking platforms. Their own websites and LinkedIn.
- Then anything else public that's relevant.

Last, work out the shape of the TAM.
The possibilities are endless. Here are some ideas for what you might want to capture:
- Headcount, plus a size band you can sort by.
- How many locations they have, and whether they're part of a group.
- Who the decision maker is, and where you found them.
- What software they run.
- Whether a BDR or an SDR should own the account, based on size.
- Where each number came from, so you know how far to trust it.

Close to no loyalty to tools these days.

The exceptions are Claude Code and the Deepline CLI.

Everything else has to earn its place on the task at hand. The tool that gets the job done quickest, with the best quality, is the one I go to.

For anyone picking tools for an outbound team, here's my system:

- Try different tools on the task
- See what works
- When something does, scale it
- If it doesn't, move on to the next one

Even those exceptions are only a maybe.

Every tool I run is on trial. Including the ones I'd defend.

Claude Code and Deepline CLI. Even those come with a maybe.

Whatever gets the job done quickest, at the best quality, is what I use. Nothing else decides it, and that includes how long the thing has already been in the stack.

So the method is unglamorous. Try a different tool. See what works. Scale that thing when it does, and move on to another when it doesn't.

If you run an outbound team, the second half of that is the part that costs something. Scaling what works is easy to agree with. Moving on means saying out loud that a tool you already chose is not the one.

"This is the most comprehensive TAM we've ever had." A client's said that about a TAM I built of 10,500 businesses, all from public data (and for not much more than the cost of a coffee).

It runs on my Claude Max plan and a Blitz subscription, plus roughly $7 to $25 a build in everything else.

The usual TAM is a ZoomInfo or Apollo export filtered by industry and employee count, and the reps find out on the phone which accounts were worth the call.

My client sizes accounts by clinicians, and six or more is where it's worth their while. So the build counted them, and came out at:

- 14,000 locations (they were intererested in dental praftices)
- 25,000 clinicians, each a named person on the practice's own site or booking page
- 5,600 decision makers
- about 1,350 accounts with six or more clinicians, flagged before anyone reached out

To build your own TAM, I'd use Claude Code (Codex would work too).

Then:

1. Decide what makes an account worth contacting

- Clinicians, for that client
- Yours might be seats or sites - maybe something else
- Anything a business publishes about itself (or someone else about them) can be a column

2. Stack every public list the market appears on

- Wherever the businesses show up: e.g. regulators, licensing bodies, trade associations, maps, directories
- Any software the industry books or buys through. In dental, a booking platform's public rosters named the practitioners
- Check each source's terms first before using

3. Let AI read every website

- In my case, it's where many dentists name their clinicians
- Two cheap models (through OpenRouter) read 6,818 practice websites for $16.40

4. Check it before a rep touches it

- Open a sample and check each row against the business's own website. AI can make shit up
- If you have a source you trust, like a regulators count, check your totals against it

The first dental TAM took about a week to refine. It's a skill now: GP, physio, psychology, speech, OT, orthopaedics and chiro since, and every build after dental was completed in under a week.

A sales leader told me they were dreading one question: "why are we paying $40K a year for ZoomInfo".

I built a TAM of Australian dental off public data. The paid spend I can trace comes to roughly $30 to $35, plus a flat subscription for the decision-maker lookups.

It also took seven weeks.

What came out: about 10,500 businesses, 14,000 locations, 25,000 named clinicians and 5,600 decision makers.

The word that matters there is named. Every clinician is a name on the practice's own team page or booking roster, checked against the page in code. A headcount field can't tell you how many dentists work at a two-chair practice.

The association register listed one big chain at 6 locations. Its own website lists 171.

A model saying "12 dentists" was wrong far more often than a list of names checked against the page. So the models read and the code checks every name. Two cheap ones read 6,818 practice websites for $16.40, and the same job run as Claude agents worked out at about $3,397.

The seven weeks went on five drafts. It's cheap in money and expensive in hours, and ZoomInfo is the reverse.

For anyone leading an outbound team that sells into one industry, here's my system:

- Start from the regulator's or licensing body's count, so you know roughly what complete looks like.
- Stack every free list the industry has: map data, the association register, booking or scheduling platforms with public pages, government registers.
- Read each source's terms before pulling from it.
- Count chains from their own websites.
- Size every business by the named people on its own pages, booking rosters included.
- Check a small sample by hand before counting anything, then score yourself against it.
- Mark an unreadable page as unread, never as zero.
- Use the Wayback Machine for sites that no longer load.

What does the licensing body count in your market, and how close does your TAM get to it?

There's no stronger buying signal than board meeting minutes.

We recently went through 43,789 board papers across 1,541 public boards to find 52 red-hot prospects.

Board papers are a board and its senior executives putting their priorities on the record. In public. And what gets agreed is often checked at the next board meeting, so whatever they committed to has to be followed up in the meetings after it.

If you sell into public bodies, here's my system for finding those signals:

Who publishes them
- School districts and universities
- Utilities and transit
- Pension systems
- Counties and cities
- Public hospitals

Where to find them
- The board's own website, including its archive pages
- Links inside agenda PDFs
- Council meeting systems
- Meeting video captions

All of it is public, and documented by the boards themselves.

What to look for
- Current-year audit plans, audit findings and risk reports. They're all dated
- The problem you solve, in their own words

How to get through the noise
- Start with the committee that would own your problem. Some boards publish far more than you can read: one county had posted 21,184 papers
- Check every "nothing found". 604 boards once came back that way because the tool reading them had failed

We only looked at the US, but public bodies typically release documentation like this globally.

If you're not sure where your accounts publish their board minutes, send me a message and I'll point you in the right direction.

More and more outbound teams write their messaging with AI.

I've been guilty of it. And I often end up rewriting more than it would have taken to write the message myself.

Meanwhile the thing AI is good at sits underused: looking at vast amounts of data, pulling different sources together, bringing different tools together.

That's the targeting half of outbound. Working out who is worth a message at all.

The writing half, I think humans are still best at. We outsourced that as well.

If you lead an outbound team, that's the split worth checking.

The order I'd do it in:

- AI does the data work.
- Someone on the team writes the first attempt at the message. Even if it's only the structure.
- Then AI improves it and applies it across accounts.

Which half has your team handed over?

For one client, I had AI write outbound sequences.

Some went through multiple rounds of rewriting, and it was bad. Others came out much closer to right.

The rewriting was on the platform-level messaging, general in nature. The ones that came out closer sat on hyper-specific targeting.

I think a lot of that was the targeting.

When the targeting is loose, AI struggles. It makes stuff up, and there's no consistency from one message to the next.

Make it hyper-specific and the AI writes to that specificity. The messaging is often better.

If you lead an outbound team, check which sequences your reps rewrite most.

I'd still outsource the data work to AI. It's good at looking at vast amounts of data and pulling different sources together.

For the message, give it some structure first. Your own first attempt at how you'd lay it out.

Then get it to improve that, and apply it across accounts.

The AI said the customer quotes came from Gong calls.
It had made them up.

That set of sequences took about 5 rounds of rewrites. The targeted set took 2.

I had AI write both.

The generic set:

- Platform-level messaging, general in nature
- The quotes, plus other things it made up

The targeted set:

- Written to hyper-specific targeting
- The copy talked to the targeting we'd done, so it had no gaps to fill

I think a lot of the difference was the targeting.

The list is the message. AI writes to whatever the list gives it.

Give it a loose list and it fills the gaps itself. That's where the Gong quotes came from.

If you lead an outbound team, look at the sequences your reps keep rewriting.

Then look at the list behind them.

My holidays used to have client meetings in them.

Right now I probably can't take on another client.
That's a sacrifice I'm willing to make.

Back then I was at a consulting firm in New York,
at the whims of my employer and of my clients.
Meetings got booked last minute, in time zones I didn't choose.

We'd been in New York six years when our first kid was born.

We moved home to Australia, and I hadn't figured out what came next.
I got to be home for a long stretch after she was born.
I felt lucky to have that.

Going out on my own had been in the back of my mind for a while.
Moving home forced it. I did it straight away.

My hard stop is four o'clock on the days I pick up my daughter.
Her community kinder shuts at four, and my wife and I coordinate pickup.

Other days, the laptop typically closes around five.
It stays closed until the kids are in bed,
then I open it again to finish a few things.

It changed how I work for myself, too.

I need to be careful with my time, so I track it.
I put an ops system in place that shows what it goes towards:
utilisation per client against my goals, and my effective hourly rate.

Then it's about making trade-offs.

I recently told a client I couldn't make some of their meetings because of pickup.
I was comfortable saying so, because our values line up.

And no, I'm not taking the piss with it.

It's how I've intentionally structured things.

It means I get to spend more time with the kids.

8 ways I work out what software a company runs.

(Including a handful that hardly anyone uses)

1. Website code
→ A lot of tools leave a script or tag in a site's code e.g. in a booking link.
→ Pro: cheap, and probably the best fit for customer-facing tools.
→ Con: it only sees the website, so back-office tools stay invisible.
→ Effort to use: easy.
→ Used in GTM: everywhere.

2. Job ads
→ Ads list the tools candidates need to know.
→ Pro: it picks up back-office tools that never touch the website.
→ Con: it's inferred. The ad might be old, or name the tool they're leaving.
→ Effort to use: easy.
→ Used in GTM: everywhere.

3. The vendor's own proof
→ Customer logos and case studies on the vendor's site.
→ Pro: it's rarely wrong. A few vendors even publish a finder that lists every customer.
→ Con: usually small numbers, and only the happy customers.
→ Effort to use: easy.
→ Used in GTM: often.

4. Their integration and privacy pages
→ Companies name the tools they plug into, and privacy policies often list their suppliers.
→ Pro: I think it's the best evidence there is, because they wrote it.
→ Con: most never say, and it means reading a lot of pages.
→ Effort to use: medium.
→ Used in GTM: often.

5. Password reset checks
→ Put a work email into a tool's "forgot password" page and see if it answers differently.
→ Pro: it can confirm a named person has an account.
→ Con: one email at a time, and that person might get a reset email.
→ Effort to use: hard, you build it.
→ Used in GTM: rarely.

6. Login portals
→ Some tools give each customer their own address, like acme.vendor.com.
→ Pro: close to a yes or no. The portal exists or it doesn't.
→ Con: it only works for tools built that way, and some answer for any name, so test a fake one first.
→ Effort to use: hard, you build it.
→ Used in GTM: rarely.

7. DNS records
→ Every domain publishes where its email goes and which apps it verified.
→ Pro: someone had to set each record up, so it's hard to fake.
→ Probably strongest on email and security tools.
→ Con: it doesn't necessarily show live use. Old records can outlive the tool.
→ Effort to use: very hard.
→ Used in GTM: rarely.

8. Network banners
→ Scanners check every server online and log what software answers.
→ Pro: it sees software running on their own servers, like a VPN or a self-hosted system, that other methods miss.
→ Con: it's hard to tie a server to a company, and it might not show live use either.
→ Effort to use: very hard.
→ Used in GTM: rarely.

Which one I reach for depends on how the software shows up. It's often a few of them.

If a tool shows up through two of these, that gives me a lot more confidence.

Which ones have I missed?

SDR leaders: I worked out the SDR-to-AE ratio at 2,206 US software companies.

I've got a theory on why, past 1,000 employees, it stops holding.

AEs per SDR:

- 51-200 employees: 4.8
- 201-500: 4.7
- 501-1,000: 4.6
- 1,001-5,000: 6.2
- 5,001-10,000: 10.0
- 10,000+: 14.2

Below 1,000 employees, the ratio sits at about one SDR for every 4.7 AEs in every size band. If you're building an SDR team somewhere under 1,000 people, that's what your peers have.

If you're heading past 1,000, the companies already there carry fewer SDRs per AE, and the bigger they get, the fewer. By 10,000+ employees, it's a third of the coverage.

That holds with each band's 10 biggest teams taken out as well.

My bet is the pipeline changes. More demand comes in on its own, and AEs start prospecting their own named accounts.

I've increasingly seen companies push AEs towards sourcing their own deals, to get more out of the team they've already got. That's anecdotal, though.

And I only counted US profiles, so SDR teams based overseas wouldn't show up.

If you've run SDRs at a company past 1,000 people, did inbound and your AEs pick up the slack or something else?

This cold email gets deleted.

How I'd rewrite it so I'd have replied:

Subject: Three pages and no ads

"Hi Josh,

slingshotgtm.com has three pages: the homepage, a booking page and one case study. Nothing for Slingshot GTM in the LinkedIn, Google or Meta ad libraries.

So it looks like your clients come from your posts and referrals. That might be exactly how you want it.

If it is, ignore this. If it isn't, is inbound something you've ruled out, or something nobody's built yet?"

Why I'd reply to that one:

- Every line checks out. I don't run ads.
- Doesn't guess my team. There's only me.
- It asks if I want inbound.
- It's about how I win my own clients.
- No brand story. I don't care about it.

If you run SDRs, that's the bar.

The original offered to write me a few short ideas.

Writing them would have been the email.
